summary:
Luke is the longest of the four gospels, and its author — church tradition names him as Luke, the physician who traveled with Paul — tells his reader Theophilus that he has "carefully investigated everything from the beginning" in order to write "an orderly account." It is also the first half of a two-volume work — Luke-Acts — that traces the story from the birth of Jesus to the spread of the church to the heart of the Roman Empire. Luke's attention falls constantly on people at the margins: the poor, women, Samaritans, tax collectors, sinners, and outsiders of every kind. His gospel is sometimes called the gospel of the marginalized.

The opening chapters are unique to Luke and set the tone for everything that follows. Zechariah struck mute in the temple. Mary's Magnificat — a song declaring that God has scattered the proud, brought down rulers from their thrones, exalted the humble, and filled the hungry with good things. Shepherds, not magi, receive the angelic announcement. A devout man named Simeon — promised that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ — holds the infant Jesus in the temple and declares him "a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel." From the very beginning, Luke frames the story as good news for the whole world, starting from the bottom up.

Jesus' public ministry in Luke is marked by radical inclusion and stunning reversals. His inaugural sermon in Nazareth (chapter 4) announces good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, recovery of sight to the blind — and when he reminds the congregation that Elijah and Elisha ministered to Gentiles, they try to throw him off a cliff. Several parables appear only in Luke: the Good Samaritan, who shames the priest and Levite by showing mercy; the Prodigal Son, who squanders everything and is welcomed home with a feast while his dutiful older brother seethes outside; the rich man and Lazarus, separated by an unbridgeable chasm after death. Each story overturns conventional assumptions about who deserves God's favor.

Women are woven through Luke's story from beginning to end. Mary and Elizabeth are the first to proclaim what God is doing. The widow of Nain has her only son raised from the dead. A "sinful woman" wets Jesus' feet with her tears and anoints them with perfume while his Pharisee host silently objects, and Jesus declares her sins forgiven because she has loved much. Mary and Martha host Jesus in their home, and when Martha complains that Mary is sitting and listening instead of helping with the meal, Jesus takes Mary's side. Women are named among those who fund Jesus' ministry. Women are the first witnesses of the resurrection.

The journey to Jerusalem occupies nearly ten chapters of Luke (9:51-19:27), a long narrative section where Jesus teaches, heals, and steadily moves toward the cross. The passion account includes details found nowhere else: Jesus' sweat falling like drops of blood in Gethsemane, healing the ear of the high priest's servant during the arrest, telling the weeping women of Jerusalem to weep for themselves and their children, promising paradise to the criminal crucified beside him. Even on the cross, Luke's Jesus is merciful: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."

The resurrection appearances in Luke culminate in the road to Emmaus — two disciples walking with the risen Jesus for miles without recognizing him until he breaks bread at the table. Only after he vanishes do they ask each other, "Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?" Luke's gospel ends with Jesus ascending into heaven and the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy. The story is not over. It continues in Acts. But the message is already clear. In Jesus' own words: "The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost."
